country.name: India
country.tagline: A tropical wine country that prunes twice a year and harvests in the dry winter, led by the Deccan plateau around Nashik.

stats.note: OIV (May 2026): India's total vineyard is about 197 kha, the seventh largest in the world and growing about 4.6 percent a year since 2019, but almost all of it is table grapes and raisins; wine grapes cover only a few thousand hectares.

country.overview:
India has one of the world's largest and fastest-growing vineyards, but almost all of it grows table grapes and raisins; wine is a tiny, young industry, about two percent of an alcohol market dominated by whisky and beer. Its story is the story of Maharashtra, and especially of Nashik, a pilgrimage city on the Deccan plateau 180 km north-east of Mumbai that now calls itself India's wine capital.

Grapes reached India from Persia in antiquity, and Chanakya's writings in the fourth century BC mention a grape wine called madhu. The Mughals were officially abstinent but some emperors (Babur, Jahangir) loved wine; the Portuguese brought fortified wine to Goa; and under the British, Kashmir and Baramati had vineyards until phylloxera arrived in the 1890s. After independence, prohibition sentiment and policy pushed growers toward table grapes. The modern revival came in the 1980s and 1990s: Chateau Indage at Narayangaon near Pune, with help from Champagne, launched the sparkling Omar Khayyam in the mid-1980s; Kanwal Grover planted French varieties at Nandi Hills near Bangalore in 1988; and Rajeev Samant, back from Silicon Valley, founded Sula Vineyards at Nashik in 1999. Maharashtra's 2001 grape-processing policy cut taxes and licensing hurdles, and dozens of wineries opened.

Viticulture here inverts the usual calendar. Without a cold winter, vines never go dormant. Growers 'back-prune' in April, after harvest, to build canes through the monsoon, then 'forward-prune' in October so the fruit ripens in the dry, sunny winter and is picked from January to March, before the heat. In the far south, vines can crop twice a year. Altitude helps: Nashik's vineyards sit at about 600 m, Nandi Hills at about 900 m. Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel lead, alongside Tempranillo, Viognier and Sangiovese.

Today Sula, a listed company since 2022, sells more than half of India's wine and turned its estate into a tourist destination with an annual festival, SulaFest. Grover Zampa, Fratelli (Akluj, with Italian partners), York and Vallonné make serious wines; Karnataka's Nandi Hills and Bijapur (Vijayapura) are the second centre. 'Nashik Valley Wine' was registered as an Indian Geographical Indication in 2010-11, India's only wine GI.

history.title: Madhu in Chanakya's Arthashastra
history.text: The first known reference to grape wine in India appears in writings attributed to Chanakya, minister to the Mauryan emperor Chandragupta, who describes a grape wine called madhu.

history.title: Chateau Indage and Omar Khayyam
history.text: Shamrao Chougule's Chateau Indage at Narayangaon, near Pune, made India's first modern sparkling wine, Omar Khayyam, with technical help from Champagne. The company later collapsed, but it started the modern industry.

history.title: Grover at Nandi Hills
history.text: Kanwal Grover planted French varieties at Nandi Hills near Bangalore with advice from French consultants; Michel Rolland later advised the estate, which merged with Vallée de Vin (Zampa) in 2012 to form Grover Zampa.

history.title: Sula Vineyards
history.text: Rajeev Samant founded Sula Vineyards near Nashik with Californian winemaker Kerry Damskey, introducing Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc and Zinfandel. Sula became India's largest wine company.

history.title: Maharashtra wine policy
history.text: Maharashtra's grape-processing industry policy reduced excise and licensing barriers for wineries using local grapes, setting off a wave of new wineries around Nashik, Pune and Sangli.

history.title: Nashik Valley Wine GI
history.text: 'Nashik Valley Wine' was registered as a Geographical Indication under India's GI Act, the country's only wine GI.

country.classification: India's Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, allows registration of product names; 'Nashik Valley Wine' (registered in the 2010-11 year) is the only wine GI. There is no national appellation system with variety or yield rules. Alcohol policy is set state by state, and taxes and distribution rules vary widely, which shapes where wineries locate (Maharashtra and Karnataka offer incentives for local wine).
country.climate_soils: India's wine regions are tropical or subtropical, between about 13 and 20 degrees north. The monsoon brings most of the year's rain between June and September, so growers time the fruiting season for the dry winter. The Deccan plateau's basalt-derived soils (black cotton soils and red murrum) dominate in Maharashtra and northern Karnataka; Nandi Hills has red lateritic soils on granite. Altitude (about 600 m at Nashik and 900 m at Nandi Hills) keeps night temperatures down.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.note: Sula's first success and still a mainstay of fresh, off-dry whites.

grapes.name: Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: The main reds, often blended; Grover Zampa's La Réserve is Cabernet-Shiraz.

grapes.name: Tempranillo, Sangiovese, Zinfandel, Viognier
grapes.note: Varieties suited to heat that several producers have pioneered.

grapes.name: Thompson Seedless
grapes.note: The dominant table and raisin grape, which accounts for most of India's 197,000 ha.

regions.name: Nashik
regions.tagline: India's wine capital, on the Deccan plateau above the Godavari.
regions.summary: The Nashik district, especially the Dindori and Gangapur Dam areas west of the city, has the largest concentration of Indian wineries: Sula, York, Soma, Grover Zampa's Nashik operation and Vallonné at nearby Igatpuri. Vineyards sit at about 600 m on basalt soils, irrigated from the Godavari's reservoirs.
regions.history: A table-grape centre since the 1960s; Sula's arrival in 1999 and Maharashtra's 2001 policy turned it into a wine region.
regions.terroir: Tropical with a dry winter harvest; basalt-derived soils; altitude about 550 to 700 m.
regions.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Tempranillo.
regions.styles: Fresh whites, rosés, medium-bodied reds, sparkling.

regions.name: Karnataka
regions.tagline: Hillside vineyards near Bangalore and on the northern plateau.
regions.summary: Karnataka is India's second wine state, with vineyards at Nandi Hills north of Bangalore (Grover Zampa, at about 900 m) and in the hot north around Bijapur (Vijayapura) and Belgaum. The state created a Karnataka Wine Board to promote local wine.
regions.history: Grover planted at Nandi Hills in 1988.
regions.terroir: Red lateritic and granite soils at Nandi Hills; black soils in the north.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Viognier, Sauvignon Blanc.

regions.name: Pune and Solapur
regions.tagline: Where India's modern wine began, at Narayangaon, and where Italian varieties thrive at Akluj.
regions.summary: South of Nashik, the Pune district (Narayangaon, birthplace of Chateau Indage) and the Sangli-Solapur area (Akluj, home of Fratelli) are Maharashtra's other wine zones, hotter and drier, suited to Sangiovese, Cabernet and Shiraz.
regions.history: Chateau Indage's Omar Khayyam sparkling (1980s); Fratelli founded at Akluj in 2007.
regions.terroir: Semi-arid Deccan plateau, black basalt soils.
regions.grapes: Sangiovese, Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Chenin Blanc.

in-nashik-valley-wine.name: Nashik Valley Wine
in-nashik-valley-wine.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel
in-nashik-valley-wine.summary: India's only registered wine Geographical Indication, covering wines made from grapes grown in the Nashik valley of Maharashtra. Nashik, at about 600 m on the Deccan plateau, has more than 30 wineries, led by Sula Vineyards (founded 1999). Its wines are mostly fresh, fruity whites, rosés and medium-bodied reds, picked in the dry winter after the vines are pruned twice a year.
in-nashik-valley-wine.terroir: Basalt-derived soils; dry winter ripening season (harvest January to March) after the monsoon; irrigation from Godavari reservoirs.
in-nashik-valley-wine.nerd_note: Indian vineyards are 'double pruned': back-pruning in April builds the vine's wood through the monsoon, and fruit-pruning in October times ripening for the cool, dry winter.

sites.name: Sula Vineyards
sites.text: Rajeev Samant, a Stanford graduate who worked at Oracle, founded Sula on his family's land west of Nashik in 1999, naming it after his mother Sulabha. Working with Californian winemaker Kerry Damskey, he introduced Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc and Zinfandel. Sula sells more than half of India's wine, hosts the SulaFest music festival and listed on Indian stock exchanges in 2022.

sites.name: York Winery
sites.text: A family winery by the Gangapur Dam outside Nashik, founded by the Gurnani family in the late 2000s, with an Australian-trained winemaker and views over the reservoir; known for Shiraz and sparkling wine.

sites.name: Grover Zampa, Nandi Hills
sites.text: Kanwal Grover planted French varieties at Raghunathapura in the Nandi Hills north of Bangalore in 1988. Michel Rolland consulted on its wines, notably La Réserve, and the company merged with Nashik's Vallée de Vin (Zampa) in 2012.

sites.name: Fratelli, Akluj
sites.text: Founded in 2007 by Indian brothers and Italian partners, with Tuscan winemaker Piero Masi, at Akluj in the Solapur district. Fratelli made Sangiovese a success in India; its Sette is a premium red.

sites.name: Chateau Indage, Narayangaon
sites.text: The winery near Pune where Shamrao Chougule launched Omar Khayyam, India's first modern sparkling wine, in the 1980s with help from Champagne. It pioneered French varieties in India before going into liquidation in the 2010s.

sites.name: Vallonné Vineyards
sites.text: A boutique winery near Igatpuri, in the Western Ghats foothills west of Nashik, overlooking the Mukane reservoir. It is known for Cabernet, Merlot and Chenin Blanc, and its lakeside setting draws visitors from Mumbai.
